findings.code_snippet:
Start with an observed problem: a repeated failed route, a user correction, wasted work or a useful technique worth reusing. Find the instruction or tool that owns it. A successful routine task needs no retrospective.

Make the smallest change that addresses the cause. Often that means deleting a repeated rule, fixing a tool, combining duplicate instructions or changing the assignment. A local mistake may need a local fix rather than a permanent rule for every task.

Try the revised method against the original problem and relevant contrasting cases. Keep the result and its limits. Save useful guidance in the existing skill, project note or native learning store so a later relevant task can find it. Reuse evidence is recorded when reuse actually occurs.

The built page carries a small poller: every two seconds it asks the server for
the very same `plan.html` and, when the content differs from what is on the
screen, swaps the content in without a reload. The plan that changed a second
ago is visible without asking anyone to reload the page.

The poller fetches the page over HTTP. A page opened straight from the disk
(`file://`) is not allowed by the browser to fetch itself, so it stays as it was

findings.code_snippet:
def git_head(root: Path) -> str:
    completed = subprocess.run(
        ["git", "rev-parse", "HEAD"],
        cwd=root,
        check=False,
findings.finding:
subprocess.run(
        ["git", "rev-parse", "HEAD"],
        cwd=root,
        check=False,
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
        timeout=2,
    )
findings.message: subprocess module calls execute external commands. Without careful input validation, this enables command injection.
findings.remediation: Use subprocess.run() with shell=False and an explicit argument list. Validate all inputs and avoid passing user-controlled data to commands.
